utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Registrar, today we are Tuesday, the 6th of May, 2008. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution. I would like to greet Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people who are assisting us. I'm about to read out an oral decision, which is fairly short. After that, I will ask the usher to drop the blinds to bring in the witness into the courtroom. This decision is an oral decision relating to the confidentiality of exhibits that have been admitted during the testimony of Reynaud Theunens. I shall read it out in private session, since we're going to be referring to a number of documents. Registrar, let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, this witness gave just one single statement to The Hague investigators so far, and that was in 1997. And then, after that, he testified in two trials, and they proofed him for testimony in a third trial. Now, why that never took place is something I don't know, but already in 2003 I was informed of the testimony of this witness enjoying protective measures in the trial against me here. That is to say, five years ago, that's when I received the information. Now, this witness came to The Hague, and on Sunday he was subjected to the -- well, it should have been a proofing session, whereas in fact he was subjected to an interview in the capacity of a suspect, himself. He was never here before as a suspect. Now, we have a written statement by the Croatian authorities that there are no legal proceedings against him at all in Croatia underway, and I have an oral confirmation from Belgrade that there are no pending legal proceedings against him in Serbia, whereas The Hague investigators, at the beginning of the interview that was recorded by video camera, and last night at 1900 hours I received the transcript of that interview and it covers approximately 100 printed pages, they informed him that they were now interviewing him in the capacity of a suspect. He was offered the services of counsel, and a counsel was placed on standby. And then the witness said that he didn't need counsel for the time being, but if need be, he would request for counsel's assistance. This is such a flagrant example of intimidation of a witness by the Prosecutor that there is no precedence in any trials before this Tribunal thus far. Now, I don't know whether you've received the 100 pages of the transcript of the interview. If so, then I'd like to draw your attention to page 3 and 4, where, in a very official tone, he is being informed that he could be treated as a suspect, responsible for certain acts, which pursuant to the Statute of this Tribunal, he can be held accountable and tried. And then he is informed of his rights, he's read his rights, and they say, "Everything that you say will be recorded and could be used as evidence against you in later proceedings before this Tribunal, including the possibility of a trial." So the Prosecutors are lying to him in his face. There are no new trials before this Tribunal, and this Tribunal cannot do anything to this witness. But they're lying to him to try and instill fear in him and intimidate him, and I see that from the transcript later on that they didn't manage to put fear into his mind. But as the Trial Chamber, you must enforce rigorous sanctions at this attempt at intimidating the witness and instilling fear in him, because this has not happened in any trial thus far before this Tribunal. Then they go on to tell him that the tape that records the interview can be used as evidence, and he is offered the services of counsel. His response is, "As I don't know what the questions are going to be, can I change my mind later on?" So he was taken aback and didn't know what to expect either, quite obviously. And then they go on to tell him that at any time if he feels he needs the assistance of counsel, he will be given one, because he's on standby waiting somewhere, the mobile telephone is on, and he can be called in for assistance at any moment. Now, I consider, and I have no reason to fear the testimony of this witness at all, but in his previous statement there is no incriminatory matter against me. In these 100 pages from the transcript Sunday, there is not a single word in which he accuses me or the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party of anything. Quite obviously, he was never a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party himself. He met me once when I presented him with a Chetnik cockade, and that's all. And you can see this from the available material. It's all evident there. However, the OTP did try something. It tried to take the witness by surprise and to gain something for themselves, a statement against the Serbian Radical Party, a statement against me personally and so on, and that is the gist of the interview throughout. Although they cautioned him that he is a potential suspect and that these -- yet in these 100 pages, there's nothing here that can be ascribed to him as incriminatory material, so why is he then a potential suspect? We don't see that from these 100 pages of the transcript. He was told that he was a potential suspect to instill fear into him and to try to get him to try and speak the way we've seen many other witnesses, false witnesses, speak in this courtroom, not to have to mention their names. I think that as the Trial Chamber, before the beginning of the testimony of this witness, you have to take a stand in the matter, and in my opinion the OTP cannot pass without being issued sanctions for what they have done. We even see that their false expert Reynaud Theunens took part in the interview, on the one hand as a neutral and objective expert here, and on the other hand as somebody who is exerting pressure and coercion against a Prosecution witness. And we see exactly when he comes into the interview, when he joins in, it was towards the end, as an additional pressure upon the witness. So that's what I wanted to tell you before the examination-in-chief started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have a few issues related to Mr. Seselj's intervention. So the situation is as follows: This witness is coming to testify. He is a Prosecution witness. This witness has given a statement in December 1997. Seemingly, yesterday, during the proofing session, pursuant to Rules 42 and 44 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, you reckoned he was a suspect, that is, his status. I don't have the 100 or 120 pages of the transcript of the recording. Seemingly, you have recorded the questions and answers with this particular witness, pursuant to Rule 43 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And in light of Rule 43 of the Procedure and Evidence, we read as follows, and let me quote: "The content of a recording and transcript, if the suspect becomes an accused ..." According to what I have heard, we have a transcript of the recording, because we have a document, is that right, if I'm not mistaken. The accused Seselj is telling us that he has checked, and according to him, to date there are no proceedings against this person. So how does it stand today? What's his status? Why did you give him this status? What are your intentions? Let me remind you that we are in open session, so let's avoid referring to anything that might identify the witness, unless you feel that it is better to move into private session because some of your -- the answers could identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. With this issue, I might like to go into more detail, and then we might have to go into closed session. But since this issue is addressed in open session, I would like to respond publicly. And I'm sorry, I apologise in advance for my comments. They may sound vague at times, but this is only designed to protect the identity of the witness. The witness's testimony has been recorded as a potential suspect. This recording has been disclosed to Mr. Seselj yesterday. What this transcript contains -- well, the testimony of the witness in December 1997 clearly show, and I will not go into any detail here, but clearly show that he was in a particular place which is mentioned in the indictment and that he took part in a number of things. I shall not go into any detail here, since he has not testified about this topic yet. Whatever the case may be, we had reason to believe that this witness was a suspect, and that was the reason why we had made no recording in the past. We cannot -- I cannot answer that question now, why this was not done at the time, but whatever the case may be, the Prosecution felt that he should be entitled to the rights of any accused, pursuant to Rule 43 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So, of course, he cannot be prosecuted by this Tribunal, but we cannot exclude that another prosecutor in another country may wish to prosecute him and that proceedings may be instigated against him. So we don't really understand why the Prosecution would wish to intimidate its own witnesses. That is not our practice, has never been our practice, and we don't see in what way this could be justified. The only reason was to protect the witness. This is why this was done this way. These are the comments I have to make regarding this particular issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, before I give the floor to Mr. Seselj, Witness, without giving us your name, it seems that yesterday, Sunday, you had an interview with the OTP. The OTP suggested to you to be assisted by a counsel because you may, in the future, potentially be prosecuted for facts which took place in the former Yugoslavia, and in order to provide you with the adequate guarantees in case of any proceedings, a counsel has been suggested. You declined the assistance of such a lawyer. Is this how things happened yesterday or Sunday, on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Assistance of a lawyer was offered to me, but then since I do not believe that I've done anything wrong during the war, after the war, or later, I saw no reason to have a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I have one last question for you. This procedure that was observed by the Prosecutor by which you were told you could be a suspect and you may benefit from the help of a lawyer, did this have -- did this make any pressure on you or did it not have any affect on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was a bit surprised, because before, when I came here, I was never offered the services of a lawyer, so I was a bit surprised. I'm still curious about this, to find out who it is that can press criminal charges against me. I would like to find that out, if possible, after this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Having heard the Prosecutor and the witness, Mr. Seselj, what would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I point out the fact that it's been 11 years from the first time this witness was heard, and it is only now that he is being told that he's a suspect. Counsel for the Prosecution here, before you, said a few moments ago that of course it is impossible for this Court to try this witness, but then why do they lie to this witness, saying that that was a possibility? Look at the third page of the transcript, the fourth paragraph. It says: "Everything that you say will be recorded and can be used against you as evidence in some later proceedings before this Court, including a trial. Do you understand that?" That's what they told him, so they lied to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, according to me, the situation is as follows: You are saying that what happened on Sunday and on Monday intimidated the witness, that those were intimidations uttered towards him. The Presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber put questions to the witness, and he deems that, and I agree with this, that he did not undergo some intimidation. So I do not think that you can do this. You cannot say that during the proofing session, during the transcript that was made only in order to give you the right statements of the witness, this was the only reason why this was done in such a way. In other words, it would not have been done in this way in accordance to Rule 43. In accordance to Rule 43, the only thing that would have been done is to audiotape the witness. But a transcript was made so that you can get, in B/C/S or in Serbian, the right document so that you know that what happened happened. You cannot now reiterate your argument, and you cannot contest the procedure. We should start now with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, indeed, I absolutely share the opinion of my colleague. She said, rightfully so, that the witness, if he was in fact astonished by this fact, was nevertheless not intimidated, so that's a nuance there. And it would seem, and you have argued an interesting legal point, that it would seem that from what you were able to read in the sentence where the Prosecutor informs the witness of his rights, that there could be a procedure instigated against him, or that proceedings may be instigated before this Tribunal. And you say that no other cases will be heard before this Tribunal, but I think that the Prosecutor must have read the sentence which is drafted in the Rule, and the Rule -- when the Rules were made, were drafted, they did not bear in mind that the Security Council will end the mandate of this Tribunal at a certain point in time. The Prosecutor was only reading the Rule according to the text that is in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, without really noticing this problem. You raised the issue, we understand, but the question that we have to deal with, and my colleague basically explained it brilliantly, is as follows: If there is a witness that underwent some pressure because he was told that he may be considered as a suspect, the Prosecutor established a procedure because of this, and my colleague, rightfully so, said that it would seem that this procedure was instigated for you so that you can realise what the witness may have said during the proofing session so that nothing is concealed. So, basically, it would be really ridiculous if the Prosecutor wants to guarantee the rights of the witness and that he wants to inform you that he may prosecute the witness. So that is the situation. This is what I perceive -- this is how I see the situation, but what -- and now I'm speaking on behalf of my colleagues. What we would like to know is what this witness saw when he was present. What can he tell us about the volunteers, about the events that went on? That's what's really important. Now, if at some point in time it seems that the witness may have taken place [as interpreted] in some combat operations, I will myself tell him to be careful and to know that he does not have to answer questions that may incriminate him. So this is what we have before us, and as my colleague put it so well, we would like the Prosecutor to begin his examination-in-chief, unless you wish to raise another issue or something else regarding this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I would gladly admire your brilliant interpretation of legal principles, but quite simply I am not capable of doing that. There's something from deep within me that doesn't allow me to do that. There are two points here. One is the subjective one: Has the intimidation of this witness succeeded? The witness expressed his psychological state at the time as surprise, so he did not confirm that he was afraid. From these transcripts, we also see that the OTP did not achieve the result they wished to achieve. They did not question him about the possible allegations against him. They questioned him about me. And we see, on the basis of the witness's answers, that they haven't intimidated him enough. There is an objective thing involved as well, and that is that this is proof of intimidation. If you are claiming that telling a witness, 11 years after he gave a statement, that he became a suspect only two days ago, then that is really brilliant on your part, but it's not the kind of brilliance that I can admire. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are now going to start the examination-in-chief. Mr. Prosecutor, whenever you wish to move into open session, that's your prerogative. Right now, we are in open session, but if you wish to move into private session, it's your prerogative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to call you for the purposes of this trial "Witness 002." From time to time, I will also move into private session to put some questions to you, and if you feel that a question was put to you that may make you reveal your identity, you can of course request the Trial Chamber to move into private session or not to give those answers, and then the Chamber will rule on this. Now, very briefly, I would like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, could you please explain to us, what role did the media play in your decision to take part in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on TV there was quite a bit about the war conflict, especially in Croatia, especially the fighting in Vukovar at the time. I, personally, felt this patriotic pressure, that I should go and fight in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry to interrupt. You mentioned that you studied something at university. I don't know what you studied exactly, but if you went to university you must know history, you must know the history of your country. What I would like to know is the following: A Serb citizen at the time who found out that there was a conflict in Croatia, would the first reaction be to go defend his country? First of all, what was the country at the time, was it Serbia or was it the former Yugoslavia? And what did you do, in fact, exactly? It would be interesting that you tell us about it. How did you go about it, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first reason was that I felt duty-bound in terms of my oath, and I thought that all of those who had violated their oath -- all of those who had violated their oath are, in fact, rebels against Yugoslavia. At that moment, Croatia was not a recognised state. It was part of Yugoslavia. For me, they were all rebels. That was one of the reasons. There was another matter, too. Since I know the history of the former Yugoslavia and Serbia quite well, the republican borders at that time were quite doubtful as far as the Serbs were concerned, in my view. Those who created Yugoslavia did not make such borders. They were made only subsequently, in 1945, so I never considered myself to be a Croat or a citizen of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, at the time you were a Yugoslav, and you went as a Yugoslav to defend Yugoslavia. Regardless of the borders of Yugoslavia, your main interest was to defend Yugoslavia because you were under oath. You didn't tell us what oath you took exactly. Maybe you could tell us what was this oath that you took. And I would also like to know if what you did was part of a defence concept of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look. I did my military service in the army of the then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When the conflict in Vukovar started, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in existence, as far as I know. The successor of that state was the -- what was it called? The Republic of Yugoslavia, the FRY. When I gave my oath, it said that if necessary, I would lay down my life for protecting the borders of the SFRY, so I felt duty-bound in terms of my oath. However, that was not the only motive that led me to go to Vukovar. On the other hand, I felt more like a Serb than a Yugoslav. It is hard to explain this, because in our country in Yugoslavia, there were Serbs, Croats, other ethnicities, all with equal rights. Whoever wanted to could be a Yugoslav, too. No one prohibited them from doing that. My idea of being Yugoslav was to have a mixed marriage so that no one would feel bothered in any way. If there are two parents, a Serb and a Croat, then the child could say that he or she was a Yugoslav, which is a compromise, without offending either side. During the war, it even sounded like betrayal if a person said that he or she was a Yugoslav at the moment when there could be a strict statement of whether you were a Serb or a Croat. Now, I really don't know to what extent this responds to what it was that you had asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have answered very clearly, according to my expectations. I don't have any additional questions to put to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, for these precisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, you mentioned on page 21, line 10 of the transcript, that you felt a certain patriotic pressure. Could you please elaborate on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: On television, we would see pictures from the battle-front the whole time, and then in the place where I was, my friends and I would go into cafes, sing Serb songs and things like that, so I personally considered that it wasn't enough to sing songs in cafes, that what we needed to do was to go -- now, whether then or later on, there were various political parties and what kind of promotions were held, rallies on a national basis, and probably this had a great influence on everything. But from this point in time, I can't remember now exactly whether anybody wielded influence on me or what influenced me most, whether it was television programmes that existed just prior to the war, during the war and after the war. It was all general confusion, as far as I am concerned, so that the possibility for political manipulation was vast, because -- look at it this way : All we Serbs, who through force of circumstance happened to be in Croatia and had our property in Croatia, all of us, when we heard of this border, Virovitica-Karlobag, were very enthusiastic and that was quite normal. Now, whether that was realistic, whether our enthusiasm was realistic or not, that's another matter. We can only look at it from today's aspect, but at that time it was all quite different. It was something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: (redacted), you mentioned the border Karlovac-Karlobag. Could you tell us who at the time before you joined, who bandied about that idea of a border?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Prosecutor. You mentioned the name of the witness, you've mentioned it. Could we have it redacted? There is an indication that the name should be here but as what you are saying can be heard, we will prepare an order for this to be redacted. Mr. Registrar, line 15, page 24, could we have the name redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, you mentioned the border, Karlovac-Karlobag. Who, before you joined in Vukovar, had bandied about that idea of that border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, it's like this: I can't claim now when I heard about this -- well, to respond to your question, it was Mr. Seselj's idea. Whether it was somebody else's idea prior to that, I can't say. I personally think that the basic idea came from Vojvoda Misic in the 1920s, but let's leave that aside. So I heard this idea from Mr. Seselj, not personally, of course, but via television, and we all talked about it. I personally at that point in time was a great supporter of that idea, because, privately speaking, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you talked about the Vojvoda Misic. In French, we see the date -- I heard "912," and here in English it's "1920." Who is this vojvoda called "Misic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vojvoda Misic was one of the most famous Serb military leaders and, to his merit, is the famed Serb arms. Now, I don't know whether you would find it interesting for me to give a lecture in history, but what is interesting is that he was sent by the king in 1920, as far as I know, to assess the situation in Croatia and to submit a report. And it was his proposal that Yugoslavia should not be created, that the state should be broken up and that a Greater Serbia should be established, precisely within the borders, as I understand it, that Mr. Seselj mentioned later on in his political programme of the 1990s and perhaps even before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, you mentioned to us that there was perhaps a possibility of a large-scale manipulation. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: We all had, at the time, if I can put it this way, feelings of a Greater Serbia. My house was in Vukovar. It was normal and logical that as a Serb, I gravitated to the fact that it should be Serbia, especially as, in my opinion, that would have been logical, because that area of Krajina belonged to Serbia, in my view, especially -- well, if you look at Srem, the natural boundaries of Srem is in Vukovar, not on the Danube River. So on the basis of that, everything that took place, all the television programmes and all the fighting that was shown, in fact, raised, how shall I put this, combat morale and our desire to achieve -- well, I didn't think about Greater Serbia at the time. What I considered was that it should all be Yugoslavia. But as -- well, it's like this: It's very difficult for me now to talk about this in precise terms and tell you what I actually thought in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness 002, we know that you became a volunteer. What was the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of -- no, it was around the 20th, 23rd, 24th, 25th of September, perhaps, 1991. I can't give you a precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did you go when you became a volunteer? To which town did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I first went to Sid. Is this open session or closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are currently in open session. Would you like to move into closed session? Private session. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like you to clarify something, please. You told us that you had no interest in being incorporated in the army, and that is why you left and became a volunteer. Given that we've heard a lot about the volunteers here, we were told that they were part of the army. Could you shed some light on this, please? Does this mean that you were part of a group which was not part of the army, in other words, a group which was fighting and taking part in the fighting, per se, without being part of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only advantage that I could have had as a volunteer was to choose where I wanted to go to fight. Now, how volunteers were sent and how this was organised, in my case it was organised through the army, once again. And where I signed up to join the volunteers, I think that was -- well, I don't know the address, but I think it was called Kraljevica Marka Street. Anyway, whether that was under the control of the police, the milicija or the army, I'm not quite sure. I received a bus ticket to take me to the place where I was supposed to go, and that bus ticket was paid for me, so that was some sort of private arrangement, not under police or military arrangement, because they couldn't have paid for my ticket that way. In my opinion, the only advantage that I had as a volunteer was that you could choose where you wanted to go and fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, basically what you're telling us now, we hear it for the first time, and it is an important point. We can delve into this subject, actually, more in-depth. There was some text and documents shown before this Tribunal which established the following situation: During the war, and I use the word "war" and I put it in brackets, two things took place; people who were in the army and who were to be called as soldiers of the army, and then there were the reserve officers also. Something I say, and I highlight, they could be called to be drafted in the army. So these reserve soldiers were, some of them, volunteers without getting an order for a mobilisation. They could join the JNA, and in this category of volunteers, and I'm discovering it now because I did not know this until this morning, is that a volunteer was able to be drafted and go where they wanted to go, and that was your case. You were able to choose the location. Is this how things took place, when it comes to volunteers? Rather, that by showing up as a volunteer, one was given a specific location; was that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: It's -- I can answer -- I can tell you my situation, as far as I know it, and the place where I was at, how things were organised there. As to other places, I really can't say, I don't know about that, and you must understand that at that time in the former Yugoslavia there was total anarchy and disarray. Now, you mentioned -- well, we had the regular army, made up of professional officers who were salaried and soldiers who were mobilised, and I think that at the time as well there were professional soldiers, but I'm not quite sure, in small number. Then you had the reserve force. That means people who were -- how shall I put this? With respect to their military duties, they were duty-bound to report to the reserve headquarters. And when the army needed an additional unit, they would replenish their forces from these reserve forces, and they would be sent for training and exercise. Then they had volunteers, in addition to that, and when they went -- well, the point of the whole matter is they weren't paid, whereas the reserve forces, in order to take part in the war, in the fighting, they would be paid; not much, but they would be paid. So the volunteers were placed under someone's command and have the status of reservists when they went somewhere to fight. That's my understanding of the matter. Perhaps it was different. But the point of the matter was different. If you arrived somewhere as a reservist, then you had to stay in that same location and go exactly where you were ordered to go by the army. However, if you were a volunteer, you could cease being serving in the unit and said you would go home because you were there on a volunteer basis. That's my understanding of the matter. Perhaps it wasn't quite like that, but I'm telling you how I understood it and how I think things were in the unit that I was in and where I know how matters were conducted. I was an ordinary soldier, you must understand that, so I can't speak about any military laws or regulations or whatever was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you see cases where, for instance, some of your comrades, volunteers, would tell the commander of the unit, "That's it, I'm going back home, I am no longer a volunteer"? Did you ever encounter such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think there was a case when somebody would say, "I don't want to be a volunteer anymore," but some people did say that they would have to go to Novi Sad, for example, and have five or six days' rest because they were sort of distraught, mentally. And I can give you the name and surname of someone like that. In the middle of an operation, he would say that he wanted to have a rest. And I think that I say that in my statement, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am looking at the time. It would be a good idea to take a break, so we'll take a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll be in private session for a few minutes. I need to make a slight change of a technical nature to the oral decision that was handed down. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, you told us that you reached Negoslavci. On what date did you get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reached Negoslavci with the Guards Brigade on the 30th -- or the 1st of October. The 29th, the 30th. I'm not quite sure of the date. Anyway, the end of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, why did you arrive there with the Brigades Guard [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived in Sid. That's where I was sent. I was given the address of the Territorial Defence Command of Vukovar and that they would be sending me to Vukovar. When I arrived there, I was told that the Guards Brigade was supposed to go to Vukovar and that they were looking for guides for their units, and if I wanted to join them, I could. And that's what I did, I agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other volunteers like you who reached Negoslavci with the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with me, well, I can't remember exactly, but there were six or seven other volunteers, and all of them had joined up with the Guards Brigade. I think that some others came from Vukovar, two or three, to join them, those who'd already had some war experience in territorial defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you give us the names, please, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember, but generally there were young guys from Vukovar. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. How many men were there in the Guards Brigade when you reached Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that establishment-wise, the Guards Brigade numbered about 1.600 men. I'm not quite sure. I was in the military police, which numbered about 150 men at the time. Of that, 100 provided security for the Command, the command post, whereas the others were deployed and distributed among the houses that were free over there, in squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How were these 106 [as interpreted] men equipped, in military terms? What kind of weapons? What kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand this "106 men." Which 106?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I did ask how were these 1.600 men equipped, in military terms, when you reached Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Guards Brigade was a motorised brigade. It had tanks, therefore, and various combat vehicles. We arrived -- we all arrived in what we call the Pinzgauers. We were driven to Negoslavci, and I think the Guards Brigade was one of the strongest brigades within the composition of the former Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Which you reached Negoslavci, were there JNA soldiers there already? And if there were, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Negoslavci, I don't remember. I don't remember. When we arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- well, quite possibly the local Territorial Defence of Negoslavci might have been there, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. In the period that followed until the end of November 1999, could you describe to us what the Serb artillery was doing? Was there a Serb artillery? Were they firing every day, were they firing now and again? Could you tell us more about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The Serb -- when we arrived, the Serb artillery was there, but I have no idea -- I don't think the guards from the Guards Brigade but from some other brigade. I really don't know. I can't say. Anyway, they, with the -- well, for 12 or 13 -- with the exception of 12 or 13 days, when there was a ceasefire, they bombed the town throughout, nonstop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you describe the intensity of the fighting in Vukovar and the resistance level of the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my personal opinion is that they didn't put up too much resistance to us. When I arrived, to all intents and purposes, the key combat with the Croats had already ceased, the fighting was over, because on the 1st or 2nd of October, they were completely routed, as far as I know. Now, the fact that the army didn't want to advance and take control of the whole town, that was probably a matter of politics, so that when we went to clean up the streets, as we called it, we didn't come across any significant resistance. There were some fighting, but not any major battles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you clarify this, please, for us? You said that the artillery was firing incessantly. Why was this artillery firing if there was no resistance on the part of the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to answer, why they were bombing all the time. Well, I just assumed that there was some political reason to destroy the city completely, and I don't really see how this worked in favour of the Serbs at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How long did you stay, all in all, in Negoslavci with the JNA; one week, two weeks, one month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was active under the Guards Brigade for 20 days. I have to say that I had to sign a contract with them, because when I arrived as a volunteer, in order for me to be a member of the Guards Brigade, I had to sign a contract. Unfortunately, there was a single copy only. And when I complained about that, when I asked why I couldn't get a copy of my own, I was told that I could only sign or not sign, and if I wouldn't sign, I could pack my things and go home. Within the Guards Brigade, now, I don't know exactly how long it was that I was in Negoslavci. I think that on the 1st of October, we went to Vukovar, and I was there for about 15 days in Vukovar with the Guards Brigade. And when we withdrew the second time from Vukovar, in order for a new shift to come in, then I got a day of furlough. Then I went to Sid, and when I returned, I had a conflict with some other soldiers in the Guards Brigade so I was transferred from the Guards Brigade to the Territorial Defence. So I don't know exactly how long I was in the Guards Brigade in Negoslavci, but altogether about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. This question might be difficult for you to answer. You mentioned 20 days, approximately, with the Guards Brigade. Now, date-wise, where would we stand then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 26th of September, up until the 30th of September, roughly, I was with the Guards Brigade in Sid. And then sometime from the 1st of October until sometime around the 20th of October, I was in Negoslavci and in Vukovar. It was something like that. Now, I really cannot say how long it was that we were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned having signed a contract. Do you remember anything about the content of this contract, what was written in this contract? I understood that you didn't have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, roughly, in case of wounding, or death, or something happens, the explanation was that this was some kind of insurance for me. But since I said straightaway that if it's insurance for me, then I should have a copy of my own, I didn't see any logic in having a single copy. If the army was to keep that copy, I don't see what kind of insurance that would be for me. So I assume -- well, on the other hand, I assumed that all who joined the Guards Brigade as volunteers had to be registered. In order to be within the Guards Brigade, they had to sign some kind of contract with the Guards Brigade. Then, probably this was the case with any regular military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Whilst you were with the Guards Brigade, what stories had been circulated about what the Croatians were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned earlier on in my statement that these were stories that were probably supposed to stimulate the soldiers in a way. They were quite incredible, especially to me at that point in time. There was one story about the Croats crucifying a pregnant woman near Mitnica, cutting her abdomen and trampling her baby to death before her own eyes as she was dying. There was yet another story that an elderly woman, when she invited the young soldiers in for a cup of coffee, and she went to the kitchen and then threw a hand grenade into the room and in fact killed them. Then there was another story that this other older woman climbed onto a roof and used a sniper to fire at the military. Knowing my own grandmother, who was not capable of climbing up to the attic, I didn't take these stories seriously, but I know that these stories had a very unfavorable effect on the other soldiers, because then in the Guards Brigade there were young men of 18 or 19 only, and it was very, very bad if somebody would offer coffee to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us who was behind these stories that were being circulated in the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well -- well, look. I assume that they had to have someone who was like a political commissar who was in charge of army morale. Well, I wouldn't know the exact name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you talk to us in detail about the psychological impact that these stories had on the conscripts and the young soldiers? You mentioned this, but could you develop this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the unit that I was in, the squad that I was in, I tried to explain this to them, that it's not the fault of every old woman who invites us in for a coffee. Perhaps we should be a bit more cautious, in terms of accepting an invitation to have a cup of coffee, but it doesn't have to mean that every old woman is ill-intentioned. It wasn't real easy to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand your reaction, but what was the psychological impact on these men? I mean the psychological impact of these stories on these men. What kind of atmosphere did this generate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look. They were afraid. They were quite scared. And in my estimate - I cannot say anything for sure - but it was easier for them to shoot now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Have you heard stories about Dr. Bosanac from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were these stories going around that as for the captured Serbs or soldiers, she was taking their body organs or blood and that these body organs were being sold abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you believe these stories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not believe that, because I knew then, in fact, that Ms. -- Dr. Bosanac was a pediatrician, so she wasn't really trained to take people's organs out. The problem wasn't in taking an organ. The problem was for the organ to be functional afterwards, in order to be sent elsewhere and transplanted elsewhere, a special technology was needed, and I don't think they had that at the Vukovar Hospital. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would now like to display the video. On the 65 ter list, this is Exhibit number 6012, video 6012. This is an excerpt of a video that has already been admitted under Exhibit number P21. We don't have the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, while we're waiting for the sound, let me just say that I only have this paper in English, not in Serbian. And roughly two more documents that were envisaged for today, the situation is the same. For most, I have a translation, but for two, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dutertre, it seems the accused does not have this in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this was an exhibit that has already been admitted, I assumed this had been disclosed, but I can print out a copy for him if he doesn't have one on him today. If need be, I can move on to other questions and get back to this video afterwards, but this has already been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume the woman we see speaks the language of the accused, so it may not be necessary, but let's give this copy to Mr. Seselj since the Registrar has printed this out. Let's give it to him. I'd like to thank the Registrar for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the problem is not that it was exhibited earlier and that it was disclosed to me earlier on, but you instructed the OTP to provide a binder for each and every witness. I don't really have to search through piles of material every time. I did not ask for a delay or anything. I used a moment, when technical problems were being resolved, to make this known; not more, not less. I'm not asking for a delay. I'm not asking for anything else. I can follow the footage as soon as it appears. It hasn't appeared on my screen yet. I can follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we see the footage now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just wondering whether we shouldn't redact lines 4, 5, on page 40, since these pages might contain information that could identify the witness. Page 40, lines 4 and 5. It pertains to the witness's occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall issue an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could show this video now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: "Unknown Chetnik: We can only fight with them." "Reporter: Why?" "Unknown Chetnik: Why? Because they kill our people. They kill our children. We have never seen the kid of two years old with the head, with head of the kid is on the pig, you know. And head of the pig is on the kid's body. You know what's that mean? Have you ever see that? No? With that people we discuss? Never. Only fight to the end. To the last -- the last bullet, the last Ustasha, you know."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, where was this video shot, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar, towards the end of the war, at the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What would be your comment on the running commentary we hear, or when we hear the man talking about the body of a pig put together with a baby's head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look. I don't know what to say. It's hard for me to make any comments in respect of that. First of all, quite simply, I don't believe that any such thing ever happened. However, if it did happen, then it's terrible. If this kind of footage appeared on TV, that would make all hell break loose. Of course, many people would be very upset and want to fight or to take revenge for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour -- Judges. I think that the Prosecutor first had to identify this footage for the witness, because the witness confirmed in his original statement and during the questioning on Sunday that volunteers of the Serb Radical Party all had new camouflage uniforms. Here we see a man who's making a statement, and he's not wearing a camouflage uniform, he's wearing a classical military uniform. Now the Prosecutor is putting this as if it were the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. So this is manipulation, perfidious manipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I did not understand that the Prosecution was showing this man and this woman as being members of the Serbian Radical Party. That's not what I understood. Prosecutor, now, you would like to respond to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution has never indicated at this hearing that the people shown on this video belonged to one or other group. We are just providing the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have just seen a video clip which we've seen with other witnesses already. The people we see on this video, according to you, which unit did these people belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd have to see the clip once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I was listening, I mean, the thing about the child was a bit confusing, so I wasn't really thinking about whether this person had any kind of insignia on or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see the video again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation) "Unknown Chetnik: We can only fight with them." "Reporter: Why?" "Unknown Chetnik: Why? Because they kill our people. They kill our children. You have never seen a kid of two years old with the head of the kid is on the pig, you know, and here the pig is on the kid's body. You know what's that mean? Have you ever see that? No? With that people we discuss? Never, only fight to the end, to the last -- the last bullet. The last Ustasha, you know. It's everything."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first girl is a Serb, I assume, and a member of some Serb volunteer unit. I see she's wearing a cockade, but that doesn't have to signify who it is that she belongs to. The young man after her, he has no insignia, and he can easily be either a Serb or a Croat. As I was observing the rest in this footage, they could be some kind of reservists or volunteers. They could even be territorials. I saw a helmet with some strange insignia. We did not have such helmets. They could have been ZNGs. I have no idea. I can just speak with certainty about the first girl I saw. At the end, there is this moment when the person says, "Well, then, we can go and join the Chetniks." Well, what are they?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another two objections, Mr. President. I heard the person say, "Let's go to the company," not, "Let's go join the Chetniks." Maybe the witness mis-heard, but I just mind the pasting of two different fragments. The first girl could be a volunteer of the Serb Radical Party. I cannot say. I don't know them all by heart. She's in camouflage uniform. The second fragment that is artificially pasted to the first one shows a group of soldiers wearing classical military uniforms. So the footage was not all shot in one place. These are two fragments artificially pasted together. That is my objection regarding manipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the transcript, what Mr. Seselj just mentioned is something that I had noticed myself as well. When we see the young woman, that sequence is immediately followed by another sequence or a clip with men, and those two are not shot at the same time and certainly not in the same premises, and they are pasted together. The second sequence that we see comes after the first one, but is not shot at the same place. What we can also notice is that young woman is wearing a camouflage uniform, and she seems to belong to a well-equipped unit, whereas compared to the second clip, which shows us a group of men, it seems that they're wearing various uniforms, and I've even noticed their shoes. I noticed that they did not wear the same shoes. Some men wear a bandana on their heads, other men have helmets, and they are wearing clothes that are quite different from one to the other. And what I would like to know, Witness, you were in Vukovar and you can confirm to us or not what I just noticed on this video. We can get the impression that the people we just saw here are quite excited. They're all -- they have harsh words, they're using harsh language. Was that the general state of mind? Everybody who was present on the premises, were they all sharing this state of mind, which can be understood because of various circumstances? But what we see on this video, is that the state of mind that predominated at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can agree with you -- well, you see, the first part of the footage, it's like a political programme. It is put in a very nice, cultured way. Now, the second part of the footage. Now, if the cameramen were taking pictures of this, why didn't they take pictures of this case -- I mean, of this child's head that was put on a pig's body, whatever? So these are the stories that I told you about earlier on. Somebody starts telling stories, and then people fall into, what do I call it, a psychosis, and then afterwards they don't even know what it was that they saw with their own eyes and what they did not see. I think that the second part explains that. The point is that the Croats were not immune to that kind of thing, either. This happened among them as well. That is why I cannot identify who these people are, and I can't even identify who made this footage. I don't know. When journalists made this kind of material, they never recorded evidence. They'd always record a story, somebody's story, but never evidence. So I can just say that such stories really had an ugly effect on people, and this shows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would like to stop the video at some point, but can we pass the video again and I'll just ask we make a still at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation) "Unknown Chetnik: We can only fight with them." "Reporter: Why?" "Unknown Chetnik: Why? Because they kill our people, they kill our children. You have never seen the kid of two years old with head, the head of the kid is on the pig, you know. And the head of the pig is on the kid's body. You know what's that mean?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, would you be able to tell me, to what army do these helmets belong? We see a helmet to the right of the shoulder of the person here and people wearing helmets. These helmets belonged to what army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These helmets that are on the heads of these two people here belong to the regular Army of Yugoslavia, and it was distributed to volunteers, reservists. I can just say that the Guards Brigade did not have such helmets. They had "djiladas" [phoen]. That's where I was. In the Territorial Defence, they also had such helmets, but they also would put a white sign saying "Petrova Gora" on the helmets. So I cannot tell on the basis of the helmets. I assume they are volunteers if they are Serb soldiers. However, the third one down here, I have no idea. That was used by the Croats, that helmet. Maybe it was captured. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: The fact that these two clips are pasted together brings me to put a question to you. The second clip, can you confirm to us if it was shot in Vukovar or elsewhere? Could you tell us where it was shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really say what location. Judging by the ruins, how much is destroyed there, it could be Vukovar. And if this was taken in 1991, then Vukovar was the only town that was destroyed in similar fashion. That's the logics of it. Now, whether it's correct, I can't guarantee 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [In English] Fair enough. [Interpretation] Fair enough. You've told us, and I'll soon finish with the video, that you joined the TO. Where in Vukovar did you join the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I finished with the Guards Brigade, I found some form of transport from Negoslavci. Someone drove me to Velepromet, and then I was sent to the Territorial Defence Staff which was at Petrova Gora, and -- in a house at Petrova Gora. I went to a house there, and I was deployed from there -- or, rather, they sent me to -- well, I was told to find Miroljub. And then Miroljub, this person Miroljub, sent me to a group of Serb volunteers who had arrived from Belgrade, but they were all Montenegrins by ethnicity, and that I was supposed to be their guide. I was appointed their guide. So the first couple of days, I think we were in the Prvomajska 1st of May settlement, and then were transferred to a house in Nova Ulica Street, and the owner of the house was Rade Rkman. I think that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now move on, step by step, and let's talk about the structure of the TOs, who belonged to which unit. It may be slightly tedious and perhaps even repetitive, but I would like to be able to establish clearly who was doing what. If I understood you correctly, you've joined the TO of Petrova Gora, and now I'm going to ask you general questions as to where the units were placed. You told us that there was a TO in Negoslavci. What was their duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the TO of Negoslavci, I really don't know what their duties were. I talked to some members of that TO after the war, and I heard that for a month they were up at the line from Vucedol to Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you be able to give us the names of the people of the Negoslavci TO with whom you talked after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One man's surname was Kolaric. I can't remember his first name. Then I -- well, I think there was -- he was in the Territorial Defence Staff, he was from Vukovar, and his name was Jovica Kresovic, this one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I think that the Prosecutor is introducing some misunderstanding because he didn't follow the testimony of the witness. The TO of Negoslavci is one thing and the TO of Vukovar is another, whereas the Prosecutor is asking the witness the question as if the TO of Negoslavci was the same as the TO of Vukovar. There was no organic link between the two, but he didn't follow what the witness was saying with all due attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am following perfectly well my witness, and I'm putting these questions because I want to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, it is very important to make clear distinctions between the two TOs, the one in Vukovar and the other one in Negoslavci, so please establish this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's by putting questions to the witness that we'll be able to establish who's doing what and how. I thank Mr. Seselj for his comment, but I will get to that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, were there any TOs at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that he was under the command of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, or, rather, there was -- whether there was a squad or group or whatever, I didn't go there much so I don't really know, but they procured food because I think food and ammunition came to Velepromet, and from Velepromet it was distributed up at the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Who were the members, if you know, of the Velepromet TO? Would you be able to give us some names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Maybe you'll remember those names later. Aside from Velepromet, inside the city of Vukovar where was the TO defence in Vukovar? You mentioned Petrova Gora, but were there other TO units in Vukovar, other than in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Petrova Gora was the rear, in fact, to all intents and purposes. The Territorial Defence held the left flank of the entire line up at Vukovar so that -- well, there was Leva Supoderica, Milovo Brdo. (redacted) (redacted). That was after 1991, where the municipality building was. Now, as to the other lines, they were supposed to be held by the Guards Brigade, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get into that a little bit later. But to go back to the question that Mr. Seselj put forth, there was Negoslavci on the one hand, and it did not belong to the Vukovar TO or did they belong to the Vukovar TO? What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know what the organisation was like and the military command. I think -- I don't think they belonged to -- or, rather, I don't think they had any contact, command-wise. I think that it was the Guards Brigade that did the coordinating, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the line 16 and 17 of page 50 should be redacted, because an address appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness mentioned that there was a unit across the street from the house of the witness, so it would not be too difficult to identify the witness that way. So, Mr. Registrar, please make an order so that the page, page 50, lines 16 and 17, be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, the TO unit in Velepromet and the Petrova Gora unit, were they under the same umbrella or were they separate units? Were they all under the command of the Vukovar TO or were they acting completely separately? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So your question is whether the TO of Vukovar and the TO -- what other TO did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I want to know if the Vukovar TO encompassed the TO of Velepromet and the TO of Petrova Gora, or were they two separate things, entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was all one, that it all came under the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. That's my opinion. I really can't guarantee that it's right, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you've used one hour, for your information. You still have two more hours left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I would now like to talk about the hierarchy -- top of the hierarchy of the Vukovar TO, and it will start with a very simple question. Who was, according to you, the head of the Vukovar TO in the month of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what city was he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where was his command post; at Velepromet, at Petrova Gora, or another area in the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. He -- unless he was wounded or something, he was constantly roundabout. I don't really know. I don't know where his command post was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a specific place where he would come back, where decisions would be taken, where he would hold meetings to which you maybe took place -- took part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: The Staff had to exist somewhere, and perhaps it was somewhere at Petrova Gora. I really don't know. My unit -- the commander of my unit went to get his orders to Stanko Vujanovic's house, for instance, so that I really don't know where it was. Perhaps that was the headquarters of the Staff. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where was this house? Do you have an address? Can you tell us where it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I assume the street was called "Nova Ulica," Nova Street. Now, whether it was Nova Street or Zelina Street, I'm not quite sure. May I make an observation here, perhaps in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's move on to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I would like to show number 65 ter Exhibit 7180, please. And I would like to say, for the record, that I will ask that this map be tendered without any annotations. So I just wanted to tell you that before any annotations are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please give us a number, Mr. Registrar, for this unmarked card.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P420.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't see anything on our screens, Your Honour. Very well, it's here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, could you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 7180. Maybe we can zoom the central portion of the map, showing Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, the usher will help you to do what I'm going to ask you to do. Would you be able to show us on this map, even though I know it's not a very detailed map, the area which shows us Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is "follow logic." If this first point is the village of Negoslavci, this must then be the road, so it should be around here [indicates], around this point, thereabouts. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you be able to indicate this -- next to the circle, that area, with the letter A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I know that this map is not a very detailed map, but would you be able, approximately, to show us where the house of Mr. Stanko Vujanovic was on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you please put a "B" next to that dot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. And would you be able to put a cross so that we can differentiate the circle corresponding to A and the cross corresponding to B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, I would like to ask that this exhibit be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please, Court Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you had a more detailed map with the plan of the town, I could show you in much more exact terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get back to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, who is Dusan Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also a Territorial Defence commander. Now, there was some sort of, how shall I put this, political clash between him and Miroljub and a power struggle as to who would be the commander, and finally Miroljub won and he was the commander after that. That's how I saw it, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. And what was his involvement after Miroljub Vujovic took the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I can't guarantee, but I think he was the Petrova Gora Detachment commander. I'm not quite sure. I can't remember. Anyway, at one point he was the commander of the Petrova Gora Detachment and the commander of the Staff. Well, they were all in the Staff and the headquarters, and I wasn't really interested in what post each of them held exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. And can you remember, when did Miroljub Vujovic take command of the Vukovar TO? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably somewhere towards the end of October and beginning of November, thereabouts. I really can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small procedural point. On the transcript, we don't see the exhibit number given to the map marked by the witness. It's on page 55, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please give us the number again, the number of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be Exhibit number P421.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, would you please be able to tell us, how did Miroljub Vujovic feel? Did he consider himself to be a Chetnik, a classic soldier, a volunteer? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He considered himself to be -- well, I don't know what he considered himself to be, but I know that he should have been an officer now. He wanted to have a military career of some kind, that is certain, and I think he was given the rank of colonel by the army at some point. I can't be quite sure of that, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know who was Miroljub Vujovic's replacement in Vukovar in November of 1993 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In November 1993? I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: 1991, in fact. There's a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Leading question. We haven't come to the fact that he was replaced in any way, that Miroljub Vujovic was replaced, and now the Prosecutor is asking who the replacement was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in fact, I wanted to know what was the name of the deputy, in fact. I was not talking about a replacement, but what was the name of the deputy of Miroljub Vujovic in the month of November 1991 in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the surname was "Djankovic," and we referred to him as "Djani." I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is Miroslav Djankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is it the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think his name was Miroslav. Well, anyway, there were father and son, and they were both Djankovic. The son we referred to as "Djani," and he was Miroljub's deputy. Now, who was who and what their names were, their first names were, I might have got that mixed up. I can't quite remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And who is Mica Djankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mica, Mica would be the father, that's right, and Miroslav, then, would be the son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've clarified the top of the hierarchy of the TO. I would like to talk to the bottom of this structure, the bottom of the totem pole, which you certainly know better. How were the basic units called in Vukovar? Were they sections, groups, squads, platoons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Before you answer this question, I would just like to talk about the top of the hierarchy. You were there. You were in Vukovar. You were a soldier, a regular soldier. According to you, who had the supreme command in Vukovar? Was it a superior officer of the JNA or was it the commander of the TO? With regard to your level, how did you know, or maybe you did not know, who held the position of a supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was like this: Since I was in the Guards Brigade for the first 20 days, I knew exactly the chain. The left flank was Territorial Defence, the center and right flank should have been the Guards Brigade, and everything was under the command of the Guards Brigade, so that the main commander, according to that over there, was -- I think he was a colonel at the time, Colonel Mrksic. And afterwards, I think he was given the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, because now we're getting into military details, there was a left flank, there was a center and a right flank. The left flank was held by the TO and the center and right flank were held by the Guards Brigade. As far as you're concerned, they were all placed under the command or under the responsibility of Colonel Mrksic. Is that what you're telling us? Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, I would like to get back to my previous question. How were the basic units of the TO called? Were they called squads, sections, platoons, groups, squadrons? What was the name that was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had squads. There were about 10 of us at first, and then we were joined by another three men, so there were 13 of us, and we were subdivided into two groups. This squad was part of a company. I think that the company was supposed to number, theoretically, three or four squads, but I think there were only two that took part in the fighting. This company was supposed to be a detachment together with another company or two. That would be the hierarchy. Well, look, it's a bit hard to say anything about hierarchy because the Territorial Defence had a certain numerical level in October and a completely different one in November. As we advanced and as we were getting people out of cellars, then, for the most part, they would join the Territorial Defence later on, because all the people we got out of the cellars were primarily staying in the cellars of their own houses. That is to say, once their own houses were liberated, they were Serbs and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. In fact, I interrupted you. I'm sorry, please finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
