utterances.text: And these people would join the Territorial Defence. So in November, there were many, many more territorials. I think -- well, I heard that there were about 2.000 of them, so probably it could no longer be a detachment. It would have to be a battalion or a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. So to summarise, you were in the Petrova Gora TO as part of a squadron or a section composed of two groups; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said something, and the Prosecutor did not note it, but for me it's an interesting thing. You just said something, and this is something we hear for the first time. You just mentioned that Serbs that were in their cellars, and I imagine that if they were in their cellars, it's because there were combat operations outside, so they were probably not leaving their cellars. So then in November they went out because the situation must have changed militarily, and those people joined the TO, which explains, according to what you are saying, that the forces, between October and November, got more numerous, because in November the TO was able to get the support of many people who were first in their cellars, but when they got out of the cellars, they joined the TO. And you also quoted a number. You mentioned 2.000 people. That's on line 50 of the transcript. So should we infer from what you're saying that this Territorial Defence in Vukovar was also made up of people who, for many days or many weeks, were in their cellars at first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. It all depended on where they lived. If they lived closer to Petrova Gora, they were liberated earlier. If they lived further on towards the center, they were liberated later and then they joined later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, tell me, were you ever in contact with people who had joined the TO? Did you talk to them? Would you be able to tell us what state of mind were they in at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean those who were in the cellars and were taken out of the cellars? Well, look, for the most part these were people that were quite elderly, between the age of 45 and 60. The younger ones had fled Vukovar a lot earlier, whereas these other people stayed there to protect their houses. They had guard duty for the Territorial Defence. We, who were younger, liberated the streets, if I can put it that way, and once we would liberate something, then they would come there to act as guards. If you are talking about morale, well, they were protecting their houses, taking care of their houses. They saw that we were winning, so their morale was pretty high. Again, if you're asking whether they were thirsty for revenge or not, I didn't notice any such thing because they were in the cellars together with the Croats, for the most part. You see, not everyone was in their own basement. If you look at a few houses together, then there would be, say, one cellar that was good, that had concrete walls, a high-quality cellar, and then all the neighbours would gather in that kind of cellar because that would be much better protection than any other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You answered a question which I was about to put to you. You said that these people didn't realise that they wanted to seek revenge, and then you added something, and you say because they were in the cellars together with the Croatians. This is on line 7, page 61. Should one infer from that that whilst there was firing and shooting in Vukovar, down in the cellars the Serbs and Croatians were together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, for the most part they were together. You see, the Serbs and the Croats had an interest in being in the cellars together, because they assumed if the Croats would come, then their Croat neighbours would guarantee for them; and if the Serbs would come, then the Serb neighbours could provide guarantees for them. So they thought that they were a lot safer if they were in mixed cellars, as it were. At least that's my opinion, and that's the way it turned out to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would now like to move into private session, since we are going to be mentioning names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a quarter to 12.00. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume around five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. I don't know whether, during the break, the Prosecution has been able to find a solution to the video problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, that the usher can display it to the witness on a support medium which can be marked. So could we now show this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should this be in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Preferably, private session. Private session preferably, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, who is Stanko Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic. He was one of the commanders in the Territorial Defence. It was my understanding that his unit had had major losses sometime in the beginning of October or late in September, so ultimately he ended up with two men only. Now, whether he took part in command in the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us what his function was? Was he a squad head, or how -- what was he doing, what was his function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in his house there was a power generator, so it was the only house where there was electricity, and that is where the Staff was, in his house, for that part of the Territorial Defence. That is where squad commanders came to discuss what it was that they were to do, or, rather, to receive orders for the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can follow what you're saying in French, but the French booth was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer, Witness 002?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic's house was the only house in that area that had a power generator, the only one that had electricity, that is, so that is where the Staff was for that part of the Territorial Defence. I assume that that's where it was. I saw Captain Radic there once or twice. Squad commanders would come there to get orders, the squad leaders from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Talking about this house, who, according to you, was giving orders to these squad commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Orders were issued either by Miroljub, or if Miroljub was not there, if he was wounded or something, then they would be issued by Djani or Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Who is the person going by the nickname of Kapolo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor doesn't know how to pronounce this. He probably wanted to say Capalo, but the Prosecutor doesn't know. He hasn't learned enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's Capalo, then I know who it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, Mr. Capalo then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Capalo was a soldier in Stanko Vujanovic's unit, he and Dragica. I can't remember her last name. As far as I know, he didn't have any other soldiers; any other surviving soldiers, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us if Dragica is a woman, a man, if it's a nickname or a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a woman, and that was her first name, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us who is Pero Cigan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Pero Cigan, in fact, only after the war for the first time. When I saw him, he was, well -- well, a bodyguard, Stanko Vujanovic's bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You're saying that he was the bodyguard of Stanko Vujanovic after the war or during the war? Could you please clarify this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember him from the time during the war. I think he became that after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to refresh the memory of the witness on this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, please tell me if this rings a bell. During your hearing in December of 1997, page 10, paragraph 2, you mention the following: [In English] "Capalo is with us, with several of our men." [Interpretation] I am going to start over: [Previous translation continues] [In English] " ... with several of our men, but Birga managed to escape, even though they were shooting after him. From what I know, Birga is still alive."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Birga is the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And then you go on and say: [Previous translation continues] [In English] " ... men whom I remember is Pero, nicknamed Cigan, from Ruma or Mitrovica in Serbia." [Interpretation] Can you tell us whether you remember seeing this person during the war under the orders of Stanko Vujanovic? What you said at that hearing that I just mentioned, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not remember having seen Pero personally. The only thing I know are the stories that people were telling about him later. I don't know how relative that is or correct, whether I should talk about something that I had only heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Who is Slavko Cigan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that's one of the Ciganovic brothers. Dusan Ciganovic got killed in Vukovar at the beginning of the war. I assume this Slavko Cigan is Slavko Ciganovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Who is Nada Kalaba?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that she is Stanko Vujanovic's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. What was the relationship -- or, rather, what city was Stanko Vujanovic from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic is from Vukovar. Before the war, he was a taxi driver in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Stanko Vujanovic and the person called "Kameni"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that they were good friends before the war. It was my understanding that they are next-door neighbours, that their houses are right next to each other. During the war, they were good friends too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many times did you see them together during the war, if you saw them together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I certainly saw them a few times, say around ten. I really cannot recall now. Say around ten times. Perhaps I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What can you tell us about the relationship between Stanko Vujanovic and the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It's a leading question. The Prosecutor is supposed to ask whether there was any kind of relationship, and if he happens to get an answer in the affirmative, then he asks what kind of relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think that this is a suggestive question, but:

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What relationship, if any, existed between Stanko Vujanovic and the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of any relationship during the war or before the war, but I do know that Stanko Vujanovic after the war became a member of the Radical Party and that he was proclaimed a vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move on another group of people. I will ask you if you know their names. Who is Gidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His first name is Nikola. I know his last name is Dukic. He was a member of the Territorial Defence during the war, although I did not see him anywhere in combat. He was probably at Velepromet or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is Goran Mugosa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Mugosa, "Kustro" is his nickname. He was also a member of the Territorial Defence, but I have no idea what unit of the Territorial Defence he belonged to because he behaved, how should I put this, as a freelancer, and he strolled about. I am not aware of him receiving orders from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where was he mainly based; at Velepromet, at Negoslavci, at Petrova Gora? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I saw him in two or three actions of the Territorial Defence, but I don't know where exactly he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said that you saw him take part in actions of the Territorial Defence. Where was that, exactly; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I saw him in Prvomajska Street or the Prvomajska neighbourhood, whatever, but I really cannot remember. I know with one hundred per cent certainty that I saw him two or three times, but where it was exactly, I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is Ivica Husnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Husnik was also a member of the Territorial Defence. However, I saw him only after the war, in fact. He introduces himself as a Chetnik, although he is an ethnic Croat. Afterwards, he changed his first name and last name. I don't know exactly what his new name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that he was a member of the Territorial Defence, are you thinking of the Petrova Gora TO or do you have in mind another unit, such as Negoslavci or Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I didn't see him during the war at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Who is Predrag Dragovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That name sounds very familiar. I have an image before my eyes, but I don't know who he is. I think he was a member of the Territorial Defence, judging by the image I see before my eyes at the mention of his first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. What about Zelimir Salajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Salajic. "Gizda" is his nickname. He is from Priljevo, so I don't know. Perhaps they had a Territorial Defence of their own or perhaps they belonged to the Territorial Defence of Vukovar as well. He joined the Territorial Defence about a week before the fall of Vukovar. After the liberation, he was president of the local commune of Priljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. To what group is Jovica Peric belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovica Peric was also a member of the Territorial Defence, and I think that he was at Velepromet during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. And who is Miroljub Draca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two Dracas, one is Miroljub and one is Miroslav. I find the two of them rather confusing. One was in the Territorial Defence. I think that was Miroljub. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you talk about the Territorial Defence, is it Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petrova Gora, yes. I am not sure, because I think that he was in some logistics unit. Perhaps he was at Velepromet. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you see him during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him at Ovcara. Now, I don't know whether you mean Ovcara during the conflict or after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You talk about Ovcara in November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 20th of November, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well, so the 20th of November. Who is Nebojsa Zoric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nebojsa Zoric? During the war, he was perhaps 14 years old. I assume that he was also a member of the Territorial Defence. He died in a Croatian prison in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once again, you're talking about the TO. Could you, every time you mention the Territorial Defence, if you are thinking of Velepromet, Petrova Gora, or other, and in this particular case what TO are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him only at Ovcara, so I don't really know what Territorial Defence he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, it is time to stop the hearing for today. It is quarter past 1.00. Mr. Prosecutor, I believe that you have 45 to 50 minutes left. At least one thing is for sure, less than one hour. So please be careful to finish tomorrow within 45 minutes. Witness, you swore under oath that you will tell the truth. You are a witness of the Court now. Therefore, you will have no longer any contacts with the Prosecutor. Since we had some problems with people who would come back after their oath, I have to tell you that you should have no contact with the Prosecution. Do not phone anybody to tell them what you testified about. Please stay in your hotel room or walk around, take advantage of this beautiful weather, and you will be back tomorrow. Our hearing will start at 8.30 tomorrow morning. So the hearing is adjourned, and we shall reconvene at 8.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of May, 2008, at 8.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.15 p.m.,
